issues: All three quotes re-fetched with fetch-text.py --check: FOUND (Internet Archive capture 20251221015235 of the EUR-Lex OJ text; Commission PDF document/118115). Article 113 third paragraph point (b) does apply Chapter V (general-purpose AI models) from 2 August 2025. The Code's publication date is confirmed on digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai: 'The code was published on July 10, 2025'. The PDF's Measure 1.3 reads 'Signatories commit ... a) to employ web-crawlers that read and follow ... robots.txt ... RFC 9309', so 'commits signatories' is accurate (the Code is voluntary).

Significance overstates what changed on 2 August 2025. A text-and-data-mining reservation already had legal effect under Article 4(3) of Directive 2019/790. The AI Act adds a duty for GPAI providers to have a policy to identify and comply with it. The quoted Article 113(b) itself excepts Article 101 (fines on GPAI providers), which applies only with the rest of the Regulation from 2 August 2026. Article 111(3) gives models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 until 2 August 2027. 'Now makes ... binding' is reworded, and the transition is added to the summary with an Article 111(3) source.

fieldFixes.summary: From 2 August 2025 the AI Act's chapter on general-purpose AI models applied. Article 53(1)(c) requires providers to have a copyright policy that identifies and complies, 'including through state-of-the-art technologies', with rights reservations made under Article 4(3) of the 2019 copyright directive, which allows text-and-data-mining opt-outs by 'machine-readable means'. Providers of models already on the market before that date have until 2 August 2027 to comply. The Commission's GPAI Code of Practice, published on 10 July 2025, commits signatories to crawlers that follow robots.txt as specified in RFC 9309.
fieldFixes.significance: From August 2025 EU law required AI model providers to have a policy for detecting and honouring a publisher's machine-readable 'no'. The Commission can fine providers only from August 2026, and models already on the market have until August 2027. No comparable duty yet attaches to a person's machine-readable terms about their own data.

AP2 records a user's instructions as 'Mandates' - tamper-proof, cryptographically signed digital contracts - so that intent, cart and payment form 'a non-repudiable audit trail'.

Optional 'browser memories' let ChatGPT remember context from sites a user visits, and 'agent mode' (in preview for paid tiers) lets it act on the user's behalf while they browse. fieldFixes.summary: The Government of India notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), dated 13 November and published in the Gazette on 14 November 2025) after consultations that drew 6,915 inputs. The Consent Manager rule takes effect after one year and most other duties after eighteen months. The Rules require Consent Managers - the regulated intermediaries that help people give, manage and withdraw consent - to be companies incorporated in India, and let individuals nominate another person to exercise their rights.

issues: All three quotes FOUND (--check). The Council document ST 15698/25 is dated 'Brussels, 20 November 2025' and encloses COM(2025) 837 final dated 'Brussels, 19.11.2025'. Proposed Article 88b(2) ('Controllers shall respect the choices ...'), (4) (a standardisation request to European standardisation organisations), (5) (24 months), (6) (browsers 'which are not SMEs') and (7) (48 months) are all confirmed. Article 88c ends '... providing data subjects with an unconditional right to object to the processing of their personal data.' The EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion 2/2026 is 'Adopted on 10 February 2026'; paragraph 108 opens 'The EDPB and the EDPS strongly welcome proposed Article 88b GDPR', and paragraph 115 makes the recommendation about operating systems.

The significance's 'For the first time an EU legislative text would oblige organisations to accept a person's own machine-readable signal' ignores GDPR Article 21(5) (2016): the data subject 'may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications'. The agents slice's own argument section cites this provision. Reworded without the 'first time' claim, and a GDPR source is added.

The summary says 'large browser providers'; the text says browser providers 'which are not SMEs', which includes medium-sized firms. The summary also leaves out that Article 88b(3) exempts media service providers when providing a media service; EDPB-EDPS paragraph 116 asks the co-legislators to reconsider that exemption. Both points are corrected in the summary.

fieldFixes.summary: The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal, COM(2025) 837 of 19 November 2025, would insert Article 88b into the GDPR. Controllers' online interfaces would have to let people give consent, and refuse it or object, 'through automated and machine-readable means', and controllers would have to respect those choices (media service providers are exempt). European standardisation organisations would be asked to draft standards for interpreting the signals, and web-browser providers that are not SMEs would have to support them 48 months after entry into force. A proposed Article 88c would let AI development rely on legitimate interests, with data subjects given an 'unconditional right to object'. On 10 February 2026 the EDPB and EDPS 'strongly welcome[d]' Article 88b.
fieldFixes.significance: Since 2016 the GDPR had let people object 'by automated means using technical specifications' without requiring anyone to build for it. This text would require controllers' interfaces to accept and respect a person's own machine-readable signals, and browsers to send them - the regulatory opening an IEEE 7012 agent needs.
